claims.text: Wear–corrosion synergy in high-entropy alloys is governed jointly by lattice distortion, grain refinement, and passive-layer formation.
Combined experimental and simulation approaches can elucidate the proposed governing mechanism.
Tribo-corrosion involves the combined action of wear and corrosion.
The relevant harsh environments include high temperature, mechanical stress, and radiation exposure.
The combined action of wear and corrosion causes lattice distortion.
The combined action of wear and corrosion causes grain refinement.
The combined action of wear and corrosion causes formation of a passive layer.
Lattice distortion contributes to improved degradation resistance.
Grain refinement contributes to improved degradation resistance.
A passive layer contributes to improved corrosion resistance.
Under tribo-corrosion, the alloy will have improved overall degradation resistance because of the three proposed mediators.
Under tribo-corrosion, the alloy will exhibit improved wear resistance.
Under tribo-corrosion, the alloy will exhibit improved corrosion resistance.
The hypothesis should hold in harsh environments but may fail in mild environments where wear and corrosion are minimal.
The proposed test compares alloys with varying compositions and microstructures under harsh tribo-corrosion conditions.
No improvement in degradation resistance, or no correlation of the proposed mediators with resistance, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is an alloy not exposed to tribo-corrosion, whereas the prediction concerns resistance during tribo-corrosion and the experiment varies composition and microstructure. This does not provide a matched exposed control and therefore cannot isolate the proposed governing cause or cleanly attribute differences in wear and corrosion components.
